moves.spoken: We take White; Black meets our king's pawn with ...e5.
Let's diversify from the Italian — the knight to f3.
Black plays d6 — the Philidor.
Against the Philidor we strike with d4. It's strong because ...d6 has left Black undeveloped and boxed in his own bishop.
Black takes on d4.
We recapture with the knight on d4. Those concessions mean we open the centre to exploit them.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We simply develop the knight to c3 — no need to rush the d4-knight; once he trades it off, our queen will be perfectly safe.
Black trades on d4 and we recapture with the queen — safe, because with no knight left on b8 there's no ...c-pawn or ...Nb8 tempo to chase it.
Black develops the bishop to d7. A caution: ...c5 to hit the queen is a classic mistake here — attacking the queen isn't automatically a good thing.
We continue with the bishop to c4, pressuring f7. The queen needs no move; we're happy to provoke ...c5, which would permanently weaken the d5-square.
Black develops the knight to e7; we castle.
Black attacks the queen with the knight to c6.
We tuck the queen back to d1 — Qd5 would walk into ...Be6, Qd3 into ...Ne5, and we don't want to give up our bishop. Sometimes you retreat, and it costs nothing when your pieces are this active.
Black develops the bishop to e7.
We swing the knight to the d5 outpost — a beautiful square. We could take the bishop at our leisure, but the knight is so strong we'd rather make him be the one to take it.
Black castles.
We grab more central space with f4 — not necessarily what I'd play myself, but a lesson in how to attack.
Black plays the bishop to e6. Development isn't finished — a good moment to maneuver.
The bishop looks awkward on d2, but it's a maneuver heading for the long diagonal — not b3, which would weaken it.
Black lunges the knight to a5, hitting our bishop.
We snap off the knight, the bishop landing on a5.
Black plays b6, attacking the bishop.
We slot the bishop onto c3 — the long diagonal we were aiming for all along — a clean piece up.
Black hits our knight with c6.
Rather than move the attacked knight, we set threats — the queen to d4, forming a battery with the bishop down the long diagonal toward g7.
Black grabs the knight, a pawn recapturing on d5 — but that opens the long diagonal straight to g7.
The queen crashes into g7 — checkmate.
